hints: Think about ammonia as a base, so ask yourself whether it would accept a proton from an acid or from an alkali.
Focus on the ammonium ion itself, three of its N-H bonds are normal shared pairs but the fourth is formed when nitrogen donates its lone pair.
Compare the shapes of ammonia and the ammonium ion, and remember what happens to the bond angle when the lone pair is used up to form a fourth bond.
walkthrough:
**Recall how ammonium forms**

Think of ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, as a base with a lone pair on nitrogen. It accepts a proton, $\text{H}^+$, from an acid to become $\text{NH}_4^+$. The reverse happens with an alkali.

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$$
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Examine bonding in ammonium chloride**

Ammonium chloride is $\text{NH}_4^+\text{Cl}^-$. The attraction between the $\text{NH}_4^+$ cation and the $\text{Cl}^-$ anion is ionic.

Inside $\text{NH}_4^+$, nitrogen is bonded to four hydrogens. Three are normal covalent bonds and the fourth is a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond where N donates both electrons.

**Check shape and bond angle**

Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, is pyramidal with angle about $107^{\circ}$ because of its lone pair. Once that lone pair forms the fourth bond, $\text{NH}_4^+$ has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.

That gives a perfect tetrahedral shape with angle about $109.5^{\circ}$.

options.A: Incorrect. Ammonia is a base and reacts with acids (proton donors) to form $\text{NH}_4^+$, not with alkalis. In fact, the ammonium ion reacts with alkalis to release ammonia.
options.B: Correct. In $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ there is ionic bonding between $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$, covalent N-H bonds, and one of those four N-H bonds is specifically a co-ordinate bond formed by donation of the nitrogen lone pair to $\text{H}^+$.
options.C: Incorrect. This reverses the chemistry. The ammonium ion is already protonated, so it does not react with acids to give ammonia. It reacts with bases or alkalis: $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
options.D: Incorrect. $107^{\circ}$ is the bond angle in pyramidal ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, where the lone pair squeezes the angle. The ammonium ion, $\text{NH}_4^+$, is tetrahedral with four equal bonding pairs, so the angle is approximately $109.5^{\circ}$.
